lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Set up repo and rebase main
steps.instructions: Run `git init`, commit a `login.txt` on main, create `feature/login` with `git switch -c feature/login` and commit there, then add a commit on main touching a different file. Switch to `feature/login`, run `git rebase main`, and confirm with `git log --oneline --graph` that the history is linear.

targets.caption: Rebase replayed your feature commits onto main
Check that the history is a single straight line

explanations.topic: Goal: get main's commits into the feature branch without a merge commit
Rebase sets feature commits aside and reapplies them on main's latest commit
Why it's called rebasing: old base vs new base commit
Fast-forward merge and linear history

hints: Make sure you are on the feature branch (git switch feature/login) before rebasing.
Run git rebase main from the feature branch, not from main.
Since main's new commit touches a different file, the rebase should finish without conflicts.
Run git log --oneline --graph: you should see one straight line of '*' entries with no merge fork.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase main while still on main, which does nothing.
Changing login.txt in main's second commit, which causes an unexpected conflict in this step.
Using git merge main instead of rebase, which creates a merge commit and a non-linear graph.
Forgetting the initial commit on main before creating the branch, so 'main' doesn't exist yet.
steps.code:
git switch feature/login
git rebase main

steps.title: Check whether branch was pushed
steps.instructions: Run `git branch -a` to list local and remote branches. Only rebase if `feature/login` does not appear as a remote branch (e.g. `remotes/origin/feature/login`).

targets.caption: Your feature branch. Make sure it is not listed under remotes/.

explanations.topic: Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed
Rebasing changes commit hashes, so they no longer match the remote
Why merge is safe: it doesn't rewrite history
Use git branch -a to check whether the feature branch was pushed

hints: Run a git command that lists every branch, including remote-tracking ones.
Type `git branch -a` in the terminal from inside your repo.
Look at the lines starting with `remotes/origin/`. If your feature branch appears there, it has been pushed. Don't rebase it.
common_mistakes: Running plain `git branch`, which only shows local branches and hides remote ones.
Running the command outside the repository folder (fatal: not a git repository).
Seeing the feature branch under remotes/origin/ and rebasing anyway, which rewrites hashes that have already been shared.
Treating a stale remote list as current. If unsure, `git fetch` first so remote branches are up to date.

steps.title: Start rebase and hit conflict
steps.instructions: Make main and `feature/login` edit the same line of `login.txt` (three feature commits, where commits 1 and 3 conflict), then run `git rebase main` on `feature/login`. Run `git status` to see the rebase in progress and the conflicted file.

targets.caption: Rebase pauses on the first conflicting commit
git status confirms the rebase is paused
The file that needs manual resolution

explanations.topic: Rebase sets your commits aside and reapplies them one by one, so each commit can conflict
Choosing the new base commit at the tip of main
A conflict pauses the rebase; git status shows which commit failed and how many remain
Resolving rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts: Git places conflict markers in the files

hints: Make sure you are on the feature branch (git switch feature/login) before running git rebase main.
For a conflict, main and the feature branch must change the same line of the same file in different ways, each in its own commit.
After the rebase stops, run git status. It should say 'rebase in progress' and list the file under 'both modified'.
Keep feature commit 2 on a different file or different lines so that it applies cleanly.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase while on main instead of the feature branch.
Leaving uncommitted changes, which makes git refuse to start the rebase.
Editing different lines on main and the feature branch, so no conflict happens.
Panicking and running git rebase --abort, or committing directly, instead of resolving the conflict and continuing.
Typing git rebase origin/main when main has only local commits.

steps.title: Resolve conflict markers and stage
steps.instructions: Open `login.txt`, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers, and keep the correct lines. Run `git add login.txt` then `git status` to confirm it is staged.

targets.caption: Delete the conflict markers and keep the right code
Stage the resolved file to mark it resolved

explanations.topic: Remove the markers and pick the code that should stay
Run git add on every conflicted file to mark it resolved
Rebase uses git rebase --continue instead of git commit

hints: Open login.txt in your editor and look for the lines starting with <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>>.
The code between <<<<<<< and ======= is one side and the code between ======= and >>>>>>> is the other. Keep what should stay and delete the rest, including the marker lines.
Save the file, then run `git add login.txt`. Run `git status` to confirm it is no longer listed under 'Unmerged paths'.
common_mistakes: Leaving one of the marker lines (often =======) in the file.
Forgetting to save the file before running git add.
Running git commit instead of git add followed by git rebase --continue.
Running git add on only some of the conflicted files.
steps.code: (conflict markers <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> removed; only the lines that should stay are kept)

steps.title: Continue the rebase
steps.instructions: Run `git rebase --continue`, then in Vim press Escape and type `:wq` to keep the commit message. Git applies the non-conflicting commit and stops at the next conflict.

targets.caption: Continue the rebase instead of committing
Git stops again at the third commit's conflict

explanations.topic: Git opens Vim to edit the commit message; Esc then :wq saves and closes
Changing git's default editor
Git auto-applies non-conflicting commits and pauses at the next conflict
Third commit conflicts again, rebase pauses

hints: During a rebase you don't run git commit after staging. Use the rebase command's continue option instead.
Run `git rebase --continue`. If Vim opens, press Escape, type `:wq`, and press Enter.
If Git says you must edit all merge conflicts, run `git add <file>` on every resolved file before continuing.
When it stops again with CONFLICT, that's expected. The last commit conflicts, so the rebase pauses there.
common_mistakes: Running `git commit` instead of `git rebase --continue`.
Typing `:wq` without pressing Escape first, which inserts the text into the commit message.
Quitting Vim with `:q!`. This aborts the commit message edit, so the continue fails.
Continuing before running `git add` on the resolved files.
Running `git rebase --skip` and dropping the commit by accident.

steps.title: Resolve last conflict and finish
steps.instructions: Fix the remaining conflict in `login.txt`, `git add` it, and run `git rebase --continue`. Run `git status` to confirm you are no longer rebasing.

precision_checks.label: No rebase in progress
precision_checks.command: test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-merge)" && test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-apply)"

targets.caption: Rebase finished after the last conflict
git status no longer shows a rebase in progress

explanations.topic: No commits left, so --continue concludes the rebase
Use git status to confirm you're out of rebasing state

hints: Git paused on the last commit; run git status to see which file is listed under 'both modified'.
Open that file, remove the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, keeping the code you want, then save.
Stage it with git add <file> and run git rebase --continue (save/close the commit message editor if it opens).
Finally run git status: it should say 'On branch ...' without 'You are currently rebasing'.
common_mistakes: Running git rebase --continue before git add, which fails with 'You must edit all merge conflicts and then mark them as resolved'.
Leaving a stray ======= or >>>>>>> marker in the file and committing it.
Using git commit instead of git rebase --continue, leaving the rebase unfinished.
Running git rebase --abort by accident, which throws away the whole rebase.
Not closing the commit message editor, so the rebase appears stuck.
steps.code:
git add <conflicted-file>
git rebase --continue
git status
